text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work harder.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure in the lung arteries, making the right side of the heart work harder

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages, PAH may cause no symptoms. As the condition progresses, signs often mimic other heart and lung diseases:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical activity or exertion (such as climbing stairs or walking)
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat)

text_blocks.snippet: As the right side of the heart faces increasing strain and begins to weaken, more severe symptoms can develop:

list.snippet: Fainting or syncopal spells (especially during or after exertion)
Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, or feet
Swollen abdomen (ascites) caused by fluid retention
Bluish color on the lips and skin (cyanosis)
Hoarseness from enlarged pulmonary arteries pressing on nearby nerves

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about warning signs through the American Lung Association Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Guide.

text_blocks.snippet: If you or someone you know is experiencing these signs, tell me:

list.snippet: Who is having symptoms (and their approximate age)
When the shortness of breath or dizziness started
What specific activities trigger the symptoms

text_blocks.snippet: I can help you prepare questions to discuss with a pulmonologist or cardiologist.
